idiom_name: Play Action (Request => Result) built by an ActionBuilder
implementation_notes: Play names the roles literally: an Action is a Request => Result function built by an ActionBuilder (Action { implicit request => Ok(...) } is the shortest form), the routes file maps each URL to exactly one action method - one handler per request - and the Responder role is the Result value from play.api.mvc.Results (Ok, NotFound, Redirect, Status). Controllers are only action generators, so the domain is an injected service and the ActionBuilder is the idiomatic home for cross-cutting concerns (AuthAction, CSRF, logging). A separate responder is justified when one action must answer HTML and JSON, where a format-specific Result builder replaces the inline Ok.
pitfalls: Action.async needs an ExecutionContext: using the default one for blocking JDBC calls starves Play's thread pool - inject the right dispatcher.
Ok(value) without an implicit Writeable or ContentType fails at compile time, not at response time; provide the format-specific encoder and make JSON versus HTML explicit.
Body parsers are per action (Action(parse.json)); the AnyContent default silently ignores a request body you meant to read.

variants.name: http4s HttpRoutes with Response
variants.implementation_notes: http4s is the functional realization: an HttpRoutes[F] is a Kleisli Request => OptionT[F, Response], so each case in the DSL is one action and the Response value (Ok(...), BadRequest(...), withStatus, withEntity) is the responder; the domain returns F[...] values and never sees the http4s Request. Choose it when the stack is already tagless/cats-effect and the effect type should stay explicit; choose Play when you want the framework to own the runtime, the routes file and the view layer. The stable 0.23.x series is current; 1.x is in development.
pitfalls: Effects are lazy: a route that builds a Response outside F, or never returns it, produces no response and no error.
A blocking JDBC call inside F without blocking(...)/ContextShift starves the compute pool.
Routes are a first-match partial function: a catch-all case placed early shadows every later, more specific route.
